summary: A Cell Press news release (June 14, 2023) reports a study by Taylor Hart and Daniel Kronauer of The Rockefeller University showing that ants have a specialized brain sensory hub that processes alarm pheromones, unlike honeybees which use many brain regions. Using GCaMP calcium imaging in clonal raider ants, researchers found only a small brain section lit up in response to danger signals, yet the ants showed complex 'panic responses' such as fleeing and evacuating the nest. The study focused on female worker ants of one caste for consistency, and the researchers are now exploring division of labor among genetically identical ants.
one_line: Rockefeller University researchers found clonal raider ants have a specialized brain hub that processes alarm pheromones, triggering panic responses in the colony.
key_facts: A study published in the journal Cell on June 14, 2023 examined how danger-signaling pheromones activate a specific part of ant brains.
The study is titled 'Sparse and stereotyped encoding implicates a core glomerulus for ant alarm behavior' by Hart et al.
Lead author Taylor Hart is affiliated with The Rockefeller University.
Corresponding author Daniel Kronauer is affiliated with The Rockefeller University.
Researchers used an engineered protein called GCaMP to scan brain activity of clonal raider ants exposed to danger signals.
GCaMP attaches to calcium ions, which flare up with brain activity, and the resulting fluorescent compound can be seen on high-resolution microscopes.
Only a small section of the ants' brains lit up in response to danger signals, yet the ants still showed immediate and complex behaviors.
The behaviors were named the 'panic response' because they included fleeing, evacuating the nest, and transporting offspring to a safer location.
Clonal raider ant colonies in the wild typically have tens to hundreds of individuals, according to Hart.
Army ants, cousins of the clonal raider ants, have colonies of hundreds of thousands or millions of individuals and can be much more aggressive.
Researchers chose clonal raider ants because they are easy to control.
The study used female worker ants of one caste and role to ensure consistency.
Kronauer said, 'There seems to be a sensory hub in the ant brain that all the panic-inducing alarm pheromones feed into.'
The brain center may be more advanced than in honeybees, which prior work suggested rely on many brain parts to respond to a single pheromone.

Funders include the National Institute of General Medical Sciences, the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, the National Science Foundation, and the Kavli Neural Systems Institute.
